extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of aesthetics; artists (architects, sculptors, painters); philosophers of art
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical criteria for producing and judging works in the fine arts (architecture, sculpture, painting, landscape, horticulture), focusing on how each art reveals Platonic Ideas, the objectivity of will, and the proper means and limits of artistic expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture, as a fine art apart from utility, aims to bring to greater distinctness those Ideas which are the lowest grades of the objectivity of will (e.g., gravity, cohesion, rigidity, hardness, light).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architecture's problem is to make the conflict between gravity and rigidity appear with perfect distinctness by depriving indestructible forces of the shortest way to satisfaction and conducting them by circuitous routes (columns, arches, pillars) so the struggle becomes visible. Its purely aesthetic aim cannot go beyond revealing these lowest grades of the objectivity of will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity and adaptation of parts (architectural unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The beauty of a building lies in the obvious adaptation of every part to the stability of the whole: each part must bear just as much as it conveniently can and be supported where and to the extent necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms of parts must be determined by their end and relation to the whole (e.g., the column as simplest support). If any one part could be removed without the whole falling, the aesthetic effect is diminished. Decoration belongs properly to sculpture, not architecture, and is extraneous ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material honesty and perceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate perceptual knowledge of a building's matter (weight, rigidity, cohesion) is necessary for full aesthetic satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure is diminished if perceived material is incongruent with its appearance (e.g., thinking a building is stone but finding it pumice or wood makes it seem a sham). Architecture affects us dynamically; misrepresenting materials destroys the relation between rigidity and gravity and the perceived necessity of parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form determined by function
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of architectural elements must be directly determined by their immediate end (function) rather than arbitrary decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the column is the simplest form of support; twisted columns are tasteless; frieze, rafter, roof, dome should explain themselves from their end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of light and climate
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectural design should account for effects of light and the climate because buildings gain different aesthetic qualities in sunshine and moonlight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bright strong light makes parts and relations clearly visible; architecture also reveals the nature of light by intercepting and reflecting it via large opaque stone masses. Climate constraints affect how freely architecture can pursue aesthetic ends (mild climates enabled more freedom historically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity and symmetry are subordinate
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularity (and symmetry) partly arises from adaptation of members to the whole and to facilitate comprehension, but is of subordinate value and not always required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symmetry enhances beauty to some extent because it reveals space's constitution, but it is not invariably demanded (ruins retain beauty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Architect's task under utility constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Because architectural works are often subordinated to practical ends, the architect's merit lies in achieving pure aesthetic ends despite these constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harsh climates and necessities prescribe forms and reduce freedom; in such cases, architects may compensate by borrowing ornaments (e.g., Gothic use of sculpture). Architecture's practical support (cost, usefulness) helps secure its place among occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural vs hydraulic/artistic water distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Artistic hydraulics can unfold Ideas of fluidity and transparency analogous to architecture's revelation of rigid matter, but generally lacks the practical support that sustains architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hydraulic displays (waterfalls, fountains, lakes) reveal fluid Ideas like architecture reveals rigidity, yet they seldom combine with practical hydraulics—exceptions exist (e.g., Cascata di Trevi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Landscape-gardening's limited mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Artistic horticulture promotes multiplicity, separation, and fitting connection of natural objects, but has limited control and effect compared to architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Landscape beauty largely belongs to nature itself; gardening can assist by arranging elements so they appear distinct yet connected, but cannot overcome unfavourable natural conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective vs objective sides in pictorial arts
rubrics_metrics.description: In still life and certain architectural paintings the subjective correlative (pure contemplation, release from will) predominates; in landscape-painting the objective side (comprehension of the Idea) comes more to the front; in animal painting and sculpture the objective side predominates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the painter 'lends his eyes' the beholder shares the artist's contemplative peace; higher grades of objectivity (animals, historical subjects) make the known Idea an equally or more important source of pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal representation emphasizes species-character
rubrics_metrics.description: In representations of animals the character of the species is expressed (not individual character), producing a distinct objective pleasure because the will appears open, naïve, and untempered by intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Animals reveal manifold grades and modes of manifestation of will (life) and instruct by showing adaptations across species; the observer may gain direct contemplative knowledge from observing beasts in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of historical painting and sculpture
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical painting and sculpture aim to express directly for perception the Idea in which the will reaches the highest grade of its objectification, making the objective side of aesthetic pleasure predominant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These arts must represent both high-level Ideas and, in human representation, contend with portraying both species-beauty and individual character simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human beauty as objective expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Human beauty is the fullest objectification of will at the highest knowable grade—the Idea of man expressed completely in sensible form—and it rapidly transports the beholder into pure aesthetic contemplation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why the beautiful human form produces unspeakable satisfaction and raises us above individuality and suffering while the pure aesthetic pleasure lasts; beauty in humans is tied to complexity and harmonious coordination of parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist's anticipation of the Ideal (a priori knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: True artistic genius anticipates the Ideal (the Idea known a priori in part) and thus can recognize and express beauty beyond mere empirical imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The artist does not merely copy nature; he 'understands the half-uttered speech of nature' and articulates what nature only stammered. This anticipation enables both creation (genius) and recognition (critic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation and balance of species-character and individual character
rubrics_metrics.description: To portray man rightly one must separate the character of the species (beauty) from that of the individual (character); the individual-character shown must still be Ideal—significant relative to humanity at large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If individual character annuls species character, the result is caricature; if species character annuls the individual, the work lacks meaning. Representations aim to modify the species-ideal by individual prominence without destroying either.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace as temporal counterpart to beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Grace is the adequate representation of will through its temporal manifestation (movement and action), where every movement and position express exactly the determined act of will—performed with ease, appropriateness, and without superfluity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grace presupposes true proportion, symmetry, and a harmonious figure; it is never entirely without some degree of beauty and is essential both for sculpture and acting. Lack of grace appears as aimless bustle or wooden stiffness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of medium-specific emphases: sculpture vs painting
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture's chief concerns are beauty and grace (spatial and temporal adequacy), while painting's peculiar sphere is expression of the mind, emotion, and character (countenance, gestures, colour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty in sculpture unfolds when contemplated from multiple points; character/expression in painting is fully comprehensible only from one viewpoint (the face). Eyes and colour, outside sculpture's province, are vital to painting's depiction of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-appropriateness of expressive means (what the medium can express)
rubrics_metrics.description: An artist must not attempt to express qualities whose essence lies in another medium (e.g., the essence of shrieking lies in sound and so belongs to poetic/histrionic arts, not sculpture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representing the physical distortion of a shriek in marble sacrifices many other expressions and yields a continuous effort without effect (ridiculous). Sculpture should represent only what its medium can express effectively; shrieking can be suggested (e.g., 'vox faucibus haesit') but the sound itself is outside sculpture's province.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraiture vs ideal representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A portrait (copy of an individual with accidental qualities) differs from an ideal representation; even portraits ought to be the 'ideal of the individual', not mere slavish copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The truly artistic portrayal extracts and emphasizes what in the individual has ideal significance for humanity; purely empirical collation of beautiful parts (ancient knee/arm theory) is misguided because recognition of beauty requires an a priori element in the artist and critic.
